t: Number of Ways to Separate Numbers — Counting Non-Decreasing Digit Splits in O(n^2)
o: Insert commas into the digit string so the pieces read as a non-decreasing sequence of positive integers without leading zeros, counting all valid splittings modulo 10^9 + 7. The string "327" yields 3 | 27 and 327 — answer 2 — while any split of "094" contains a piece starting with zero, so the answer is 0. With lengths up to 3500, naive enumeration is exponential and even string-heavy O(n^3) dynamic programming is borderline. Two standard tricks close the gap: a DP over (position, length of current piece) whose transitions ask whether one substring is numerically at most another, and an LCP table that compares equal-length substrings in O(1); folding transition contributions into running suffix sums removes the last linear factor, landing at O(n^2) time and space.
k: Define dp[i][l] as the number of ways to split num[i:] when the next piece taken has exactly l digits; the answer aggregates l over the first piece.
A successor longer than the current piece is automatically numerically greater, and a shorter one automatically smaller — only equal-length successors need an actual comparison.
lcp[i][j], the longest common prefix of suffixes starting at i and j, makes equal-length comparison O(1): compare digits at position i + lcp versus j + lcp.

a.n: Approach 1: Memoized DFS with Direct String Comparison
a.i: From position i with previous piece length plen, try every next piece length l >= max(plen, 1); longer pieces are automatically numerically greater than the previous one, so only l == plen requires an actual comparison, done by slicing strings. Clear and provably correct, but each of the O(n^2) states may copy O(n) characters, so this serves small inputs and as the conceptual bridge to the optimal solution.
s: dfs(i, plen): return 1 if i == n; return 0 if num[i] is a leading zero.
Iterate l from max(plen, 1) to n - i.
Skip l == plen when the previous slice compares greater than the candidate slice.
a.t: O(n^3) worst case — O(n^2) states, each slicing or comparing up to O(n) characters
a.sp: O(n^2) for the memo plus O(n) recursion depth

a.n: Approach 2: Bottom-Up DP with LCP Table and Suffix Sums
a.i: Precompute lcp[i][j] backwards so equal-length substrings compare in O(1): A = num[i:i+l] vs B = num[j:j+l] satisfies A <= B iff their common prefix reaches length l or A holds the smaller digit at the first mismatch. Process positions right to left keeping suffix-sum rows Q[i][m] = sum of dp values for lengths m..n-i. For a piece of length l starting at i, successors live at j = i + l: strictly longer successors are automatically valid and contribute Q[j][l+1]; the equal-length successor contributes Q[j][l] - Q[j][l+1] exactly when A <= B; shorter ones can never qualify. Each row becomes a running suffix sum, so Q[0][1] is the answer.
s: Fill lcp[i][j] from bottom-right: lcp[i][j] = lcp[i+1][j+1] + 1 when num[i] == num[j], else 0.
Iterate i from right to left; leave the whole row at zero when num[i] is a leading zero.
Sweep lengths l from n - i down to 1, letting j = i + l; base case cur = 1 when j == n.
Otherwise set cur = Q[j][l+1]; if j + l <= n, use lcp to test num[i:i+l] <= num[j:j+l] and add dp[j][l] = Q[j][l] - Q[j][l+1] when true.
Accumulate a running suffix sum into Q[i][l]; the answer is Q[0][1].
a.t: O(n^2) — two triangular double loops over roughly n^2/2 pairs each
a.sp: O(n^2) — the lcp table and the suffix-sum DP rows

w: Lead with the three-way length argument: longer successors always qualify, shorter ones never do, equal lengths need one comparison — that collapses an awkward range of lengths into suffix sums. Pitfalls: letting pieces start with zero (entire DP rows must stay empty), lexicographically comparing substrings of different lengths (valid only when lengths match), getting the inequality direction backwards (the sequence must be NON-DECREASING), and recursion depth or stack limits for the memoized variant on long inputs. Follow-up: reconstruct any one valid splitting via parent pointers, or switch the requirement to a strictly increasing sequence, which turns the equal-length test into a strict comparison and forbids the equal-length tie.
